The Case for Total Zoning Abolition: Unleashing the Free Market for Human Flourishing

To own a piece of land is to hold a bundle of rights: the right to use it, to exclude others from it, and to build upon it. Yet, in modern America and much of the developed world, this fundamental tenet of private property is a carefully maintained illusion. Through the mechanism of zoning laws, municipal governments dictate precisely what a property owner can and cannot do with their own land, down to the square footage of a building, the type of business allowed, and even the architectural aesthetic. Zoning is an archaic, paternalistic imposition that violates property rights, artificially inflates the cost of living, stifles economic dynamism, and exacerbates urban sprawl. The complete and total abolition of all zoning laws is not merely a radical thought experiment; it is an economic and moral imperative that would usher in an era of unprecedented affordability, innovation, and human flourishing.

At its core, the argument against zoning begins with the moral absolute of self-ownership and private property. If an individual purchases a parcel of land, pays for it with their own labor, and maintains it with their own resources, they alone should determine its highest and best use. Zoning fundamentally severs this relationship, reducing the property owner to a tenant of the state. The government, acting as a centralized planning board, dictates whether a person can operate a bakery on the ground floor of their home, subdivide their lot to house their aging parents, or build a duplex to generate rental income. This regulatory straitjacket is a "taking" in everything but name. A society that truly values liberty cannot tolerate a system where the state holds a perpetual, unilateral veto over the peaceful use of private property.

Transitioning from the moral to the practical, the abolition of zoning is the single most effective tool for solving the modern housing crisis. For decades, local governments have used restrictive zoning—particularly single-family exclusive zoning—to artificially cap the supply of housing. By legally mandating that vast swaths of land can only contain one home per lot, governments have placed a regulatory floor under housing prices, creating an artificial scarcity that punishes the working and middle classes while enriching incumbent homeowners.

In a purely market-driven system, however, the price mechanism works to clear shortages. If demand for housing in a city surges, property values rise. In a free market, this price signal incentivizes developers and homeowners to build more densely—constructing apartment buildings, townhomes, and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) to capture the profits of high demand. This influx of supply eventually stabilizes and lowers prices. By removing zoning, we allow human ingenuity and capital to flow directly toward solving the housing shortage, transforming shelter from a luxury good back into a basic, affordable necessity.

Paradoxically, zoning advocates often claim that land-use regulations protect the "character" of a neighborhood and prevent environmental degradation. In reality, zoning is the primary engine of urban sprawl and environmental destruction. Traditional Euclidean zoning strictly separates residential, commercial, and industrial areas. Because people cannot live near where they work or shop, zoning mandates sprawling, car-dependent infrastructure. This leads to massive highways, endless pavement, the destruction of green spaces on the urban periphery, and skyrocketing carbon emissions.

Pre-zoning cities, and the few modern pockets that exist outside of strict zoning (like Houston, Texas, which has no traditional zoning, though it still suffers from some restrictive land-use ordinances), demonstrate that free markets organically create mixed-use, walkable, vibrant neighborhoods. When developers are unconstrained by arbitrary use-maps, they naturally build grocery stores at the bottom of apartment buildings and offices within walking distance of homes. The "15-minute city"—a utopian concept for modern urban planners—is effortlessly achieved by the free market when left unmolested by zoning codes.

Furthermore, zoning freezes cities in amber, protecting obsolete 20th-century land-use patterns from 21st-century realities. The rise of remote work, e-commerce, and the sharing economy has radically altered how humans live and work. Yet, zoning laws force a suburban, industrial-era lifestyle onto a population that no longer wants or needs it. Empty office buildings sit idle because developers are legally barred from converting them into desperately needed residential micro-apartments. A neighborhood that would perfectly support a corner café is legally restricted to residential use, forcing residents to drive miles for a cup of coffee. Unrestricted market-driven development is inherently adaptive; it allows resources to be rapidly reallocated to their most urgently needed purposes.

Critics of total zoning abolition inevitably rely on the "nuisance" fallacy: the fear that without zoning, a noisy, polluting factory will suddenly open next to a daycare or a suburban home. This argument fundamentally misunderstands the difference between zoning and nuisance law. Zoning is a preemptive, blanket restriction imposed by bureaucrats. Nuisance law, by contrast, is a reactive, common-law framework based on actual harm. Under a system of strong property rights, you do not have the right to emit toxic smoke or deafening noise onto your neighbor's land. If a factory truly harms a resident, the resident has legal recourse through the courts.

Moreover, the fear of incompatible uses ignores the power of private governance. In the absence of state-mandated zoning, property owners would naturally turn to private covenants, deed restrictions, and homeowners' associations to establish neighborhood rules. The crucial difference is voluntarism. Under zoning, you are forced to submit to the state’s rules. Under private covenants, you explicitly consent to a set of rules when you purchase the property, and you can choose to buy into a community with strict aesthetic rules, or a highly deregulated, dynamic area, based entirely on your own preferences.

The complete abolition of zoning is not a descent into chaos; it is a return to order based on consent, economics, and liberty. It is time to dismantle the centralized planning boards that act as gatekeepers to the American Dream. By unleashing unrestricted market-driven development, we can restore the absolute right to private property, dismantle the regulatory walls that keep housing unaffordable, end the environmentally disastrous practice of enforced sprawl, and allow our cities to dynamically evolve to meet the needs of their inhabitants. A world without zoning is a world where builders can build, where entrepreneurs can innovate, and where the fundamental right to own and use one's property is finally made real.

The core economic argument for eliminating zoning is based on the law of supply and demand: artificial restrictions on supply lead to higher prices, while freeing up supply lowers them.

  • Ending Artificial Scarcity: When zoning limits how many homes can be built in a high-demand city, the limited supply causes prices to skyrocket.   • Reducing Compliance Costs: Zoning laws come with massive indirect costs.   • Removing Mandated Amenities: Zoning often includes "inclusionary zoning" (mandating a percentage of units be affordable) or parking minimums (requiring a specific number of parking spaces per unit). Free-market advocates argue that forcing developers to build expensive underground parking or subsidize units makes all housing more expensive. 3. Respecting Property Rights

  • Preventing "Regulatory Takings": In legal terms, if the government restricts your land so heavily that you cannot use it productively, it is argued to be a "taking" without just compensation, which violates the Fifth Amendment (in the U.S.). The American city is a paradox. It recognizes that a property line is a boundary of sovereignty, not a line where the neighbor’s aesthetic preferences become binding law.

Critics argue that "externalities" justify control. But the definition of externality has been stretched to absurdity. A shadow cast by a new building is not an externality; it is the physics of the sun. A change in "neighborhood character" is not a harm; it is the inevitable evolution of a living city. If the moral argument is the foundation, the economic argument is the wrecking ball. Zoning is, in its essence, a government-mandated cartel. By restricting the supply of housing and commercial space—through height limits, density caps, parking minimums, single-family mandates, and urban growth boundaries—zoning creates artificial scarcity. In a market with inelastic supply and rising demand, the result is inevitable: stratospheric rents and home prices.

It turns housing into a speculative asset class rather than a consumable good. In a free market, development rights are inherent to the land, not a scarcity commodity rationed by bureaucrats. The call to abolish zoning is not a call for anarchy; it is a call for the rule of law over the rule of men. It is a recognition that the "neighborhood character" worth preserving is not the physical envelope of the buildings, but the vitality, diversity, and affordability of the human life within them.

The result is a housing crisis that impoverishes the working class, a climate crisis fueled by mandated sprawl, a segregation crisis etched into the map, and a liberty crisis where a homeowner needs a permit to build a shed. The invisible fence must come down. Let the market build. Let the people choose. Let the city breathe. Abolish zoning now.

This vacates their previous "mid-tier" housing, which becomes available to middle-income households, cascading down to free up the oldest, most affordable stock. Zoning breaks this chain by preventing new luxury supply, forcing the wealthy to bid up existing older stock ("reverse filtering").
  • Competition Among Landlords: A surge in total units shifts bargaining power from landlords to tenants. Vacancy rates rise, concessions (free months rent, reduced deposits) appear, and rent growth stabilizes or declines relative to income.
  • Innovation in Construction: Without prescriptive codes dictating form (e.g., minimum lot sizes, mandatory parking structures, aesthetic mandates), builders can experiment with cheaper construction methods: modular/prefab housing, single-stair residential buildings (common globally, banned in much of US), micro-units, and co-living arrangements.

  3. Market Mechanisms (Insurance/Financing): Lenders and insurers would require safety standards (fire separation, structural integrity) as conditions for capital, effectively enforcing building safety codes without government zoning use codes.

The case for total zoning elimination posits that scarcity is manufactured by law. By treating housing as a market good rather than a controlled commodity, proponents argue we would see:

Eliminating these separations would allow for more housing to be built near where people work and want to live, reducing transportation costs and making housing more affordable in a holistic sense.

3. Greater Respect for Property Rights:

  • Freedom to Use One's Property: A core tenet of property rights is the owner's ability to use their land as they see fit, within the bounds of not harming others. Zoning laws, by their nature, restrict this freedom, dictating what can and cannot be built regardless of the landowner's desires or the economic potential of the property. Abolitionists argue that this infringes upon a fundamental right.
  • Individual Autonomy: Property owners should have the autonomy to decide how to utilize their assets. Whether they want to build a modest home, a duplex, or a small apartment building on their land should be their decision, not one dictated by a government zoning code.

How Removing All Government Land Use Regulations Could Achieve These:

The core mechanism by which eliminating zoning is supposed to achieve these benefits is by removing artificial constraints on the built environment. Without zoning, the decisions about what gets built, where it gets built, and in what form it gets built would primarily be driven by:

For libertarian and free-market advocates, the strongest argument against zoning is philosophical. They view government land-use regulations as an unjust infringement on private property rights:

  • The Principle of Ownership: Proponents argue that if an individual owns a piece of land, they should have the right to use, develop, or sell it as they see fit, provided they do not cause direct, physical harm to their neighbors.

In cities like Houston, Texas—America’s largest city without formal zoning—housing costs remain significantly lower than in comparable cities with strict regulations. Zoning laws create artificial scarcity and inefficiency by preventing land from being used in the way that maximizes its value. A parcel of land may be ideally located near transit, schools, and jobs, but if it’s zoned "R-1 Single-Family," it cannot host a grocery store, a clinic, or a small business—regardless of community need. This rigidity prevents organic economic development and forces commercial activity into isolated zones farther from residents, increasing car dependency and commute times.

By removing zoning, the market—guided by consumer behavior and property owners’ self-interest—would determine the most efficient use of land. A store might open in a converted garage because local demand exists. A homeowner might split their property to include a basement rentals or an accessory dwelling unit, gaining income and helping a young family find affordable housing. These are decisions made not by bureaucratic planners in city hall, but by individuals responding to real needs. Market signals, not central planners, should determine where a coffee shop should go or how many bedrooms a home needs.

3. Zoning Enforces Economic and Racial Segregation

Zoning was born in the early 20th century with racially discriminatory origins—initially implemented to enforce racial segregation under the guise of land use. Explicitly “racial covenants” were later replaced by "economic" zoning laws that functioned the same way: by banning multi-family housing and mandating large lot sizes, zoning excluded lower-income households, overwhelmingly people of color, from wealthier neighborhoods. While explicit racial covenants are gone, the legacy remains.

Today, zoning continues to protect the privilege of affluent homeowners at the expense of upward mobility. It entrenches inequality by preventing denser, mixed-income housing that could reduce housing costs and promote integration. Abolishing zoning would eliminate this structural barrier, allowing for greater socioeconomic diversity. As research from economists like Raj Chetty shows, children in more integrated, mixed-income neighborhoods have better long-term outcomes. By allowing unrestricted development, we open doors not just to property, but to opportunity.

4. Zoning Protects NIMBYism, Not Communities

Zoning is often justified as a way to preserve neighborhood character. But “preserving character” is a euphemism for NIMBYism ("Not In My Backyard")—the social power of existing property owners to veto new development that might affect their view, their property value, or their personal comfort. This self-serving veto culture distorts democratic priorities, favoring narrow interests over the public good.

When homeowners block new apartments to preserve quiet or privacy, they ignore the 10,000 people waiting for housing, the essential workers who cannot afford to live near their jobs, and the environmental cost of sprawl and long commutes. Abolishing zoning transfers power from insiders (current owners) to outsiders (future renters and new residents), prioritizing inclusion and dynamism over stagnation and exclusion.

5. The Market Manages Externalities Better Than Bureaucrats

Critics argue that zoning is necessary to prevent externalities—like noise, crowding, and environmental damage. But this confuses zoning with property-specific regulation. Unlike rigid, one-size-fits-all zoning, market mechanisms and efficient regulatory alternatives exist to manage externalities without micromanaging land use.

For example:

  • Contractual covenants and homeowners’ agreements can prevent buildings from, say, running a loud factory next to a quiet home.
  • Nuisance laws can penalize actual harms (e.g., noise, pollution) rather than regulating hypothetical ones.
  • Building codes and environmental standards ensure safety, accessibility, and sustainability regardless of zoning type.
  • Insurance markets, fire codes, and occupancy laws already govern safety concerns that zoning claims to address.

Private homeowners and developers, negotiating with residents and tenants, are more agile and responsive than zoning boards. A restaurant can open next to a house, but if it generates noise, the market resolves it efficiently: tenants move out (and pay less for a noisy location), the owner modifies their operations, or they convert to a quieter use. The flexibility of market-based solutions allows for context-sensitive, real-time adaptation—unlike static zoning maps that change once a decade, if at all.

6. Environmental Benefits of Organic, Dense, Transit-Friendly Development

Zoning-induced sprawl—encouraged by mandatory large lots, single-use districts, and parking minimums—increases car dependency and carbon emissions. By contrast, deregulated development allows organic, transit-adjacent, dense neighborhoods to emerge naturally. When people are free to build where the market needs it, mixed-use, walkable communities develop organically: homes near jobs, shops beside offices, schools near parks.

Studies show that unfettered development tends toward higher density and shorter commutes in response to high prices and congestion. Consider Tokyo—a city with minimal zoning since WWII, where property owners can freely combine residential, commercial, and light industrial uses. Tokyo has the lowest CO₂ emissions per capita among major global cities, affordable housing, and some of the world’s highest population density—without the American-style housing disaster. Its citizens enjoy unprecedented mobility, affordability, and choice.

7. Property Rights Are Fundamental Rights

At its core, the abolition of zoning returns to a foundational American principle: ownership includes the right to use one’s property wisely. Abolishing zoning restores the full bundle of property rights stripped by the state. If a person owns a home, they should have the freedom to build a second story, add an apartment for a family, start a home business, or turn their garage into a studio—without asking permission from a planning board.

This is not anarchy. It is liberty. As legal scholars and economists from Henry George to Hernando de Soto have argued, secure, transferable property rights are the engine of prosperity. Restricting those rights in the name of "planning" is a form of state overreach that diminishes economic vitality and civic agency.

Addressing Common Objections

  • "Won’t cities descend into chaos?"
    No. Market order emerges through contracts, norms, and competition. Just as open markets for food or fashion don’t lead to chaos, open land use thrives through mutual benefit. Spontaneous order is more flexible and adaptive than top-down control.

  • "What about health and safety?"
    Again, zoning is not the only tool. Building codes, fire codes, nuisance laws, environmental regulation, and fire insurance requirements already address physical risks—without restricting economic possibility.

  • "Won’t it destroy suburbs?"
    Suburbs may evolve—but not vanish. A homeowner might convert their home into a fourplex, but others might maintain single-family homes. Choice returns to the market. Communities will always reflect demand, not mandates.

  • "Developers will exploit it."
    Developers already exploit the scarcity created by zoning by lobbying for variances and subsidies. A free market rewards service, not privilege. Competition ensures quality and value.

Conclusion

Zoning laws have outlived their purpose and now serve primarily to entrench inequality, suppress supply, and slow progress. Rather than cure the ills of urban life—density, nuisance, sprawl—they create and amplify them. Abolishing zoning laws is not a surrender to disorder, but a return to functional markets, personal freedom, environmental sustainability, and social justice.

By fully restoring private property rights and allowing market-driven development, we can solve the housing crisis, promote inclusive communities, reduce emissions, and unleash a new era of civic and economic vitality. The tragedy of zoning is not that we lack control over our cities—it is that we have given control to bureaucratic plans instead of people and markets.

The future of American cities—and of urban life worldwide—is dense, diverse, dynamic, and open. Abolish zoning. Let the market build for the people, not the planners. The rewards will be affordable homes, dynamic innovation, and a freer, more just society. The time for reform is now. Unzoned is the way forward.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for completely eliminating zoning laws, describing how removing all government land use regulations could improve housing availability, affordability, and respect for property rights.
Model Response:

Completely eliminating zoning laws—government land use regulations that dictate how properties can be used (e.g., residential, commercial, industrial, density, height limits)—is a controversial but increasingly debated topic in urban economics and housing policy. Advocates argue that removing or drastically reducing zoning laws could yield significant benefits in housing availability, affordability, and property rights, while critics warn of potential downsides (which we’ll touch on briefly). Below are the key supposed benefits and reasoning behind abolishing zoning laws entirely, grounded in free-market, libertarian, and supply-side economic principles:

1. Increased Housing Supply & Availability

Benefit:
Zoning laws often limit the number of homes that can be built on a given plot (e.g., single-family-only zones, minimum lot sizes, restrictions on accessory dwelling units). Removing these rules allows landowners to build according to market demand.

  • Denser development becomes possible: Without density restrictions, owners could build multi-family units, townhouses, or small apartments on land currently limited to single-family homes.
  • Elimination of NIMBYism (Not In My Backyard): Critics argue that zoning laws, especially single-family zoning, are used to exclude multifamily housing and prevent higher-density development, keeping housing scarce and expensive.
  • Naturally adaptive housing mix: Property owners could respond quickly to market signals—building more housing where demand is highest—leading to a more diverse and responsive supply.

> Example: In cities like Tokyo (which has lenient zoning), owners can convert homes into apartments, build micro-units, or even replace small homes with mid-rise buildings without special permission. This has helped keep housing prices relatively low compared to similarly sized global cities.

2. Housing Affordability

Benefit:
Supply and demand: when the supply of housing increases, prices drop or grow more slowly.

  • Reduced artificial scarcity: Zoning limits housing density and types, creating artificial scarcity, which drives up prices. Removing these constraints allows more units to be built, increasing competition and lowering rents and home prices.
  • Faster adaptation to population growth: Cities could scale housing stock quickly in response to population or job growth, reducing price spikes.
  • More affordable unit types: Without bans on basement apartments, in-law units, or tiny homes (often prohibited by zoning), more affordable entry-level housing becomes possible "organically."

> Evidence: Researchers like economist Edward Glaeser (Harvard) and urbanist Matthew Yglesias have shown that strict zoning in cities like San Francisco, New York, and Los Angeles contributes to severe affordability crises. Where cities legalize more housing (e.g., Oregon’s state reform ending single-family zoning), prices grow more slowly.

3. Greater Innovation and Mix of Uses

Benefit:
Zoning separates residential, commercial, and industrial uses, making cities less dynamic.

  • Mixed-use development becomes legal: Without use restrictions, people could run businesses from homes, convert storefronts into apartments, or open childcare centers in quiet neighborhoods—adapting spaces to actual need.
  • Revitalization of underused land: Vacant lots, outdated commercial buildings, and single-family homes could be redeveloped flexibly (e.g., a small office over a garage, a café in a home).
  • Entrepreneurial opportunity: Individuals could adapt property for niche markets (e.g., micro-housing for seniors, home bakeries, shared workspaces).

> Example: In Houston (which has no traditional zoning but regulates land use via form-based codes and private covenants), neighborhoods have evolved organically with home shops, duplexes, and commercial buildings without the rigidity of conventional zoning.

4. Respect for Property Rights

Benefit:
Zoning laws restrict what a landowner can do with their own property, treating owners as tenants of the state rather than sovereigns of their capital.

  • Property as a bundle of rights: A core libertarian principle is that owners should control their property unless it directly harms others (nuisance). Zoning extends beyond traditional nuisance law (e.g., sound, pollution) to regulate use, aesthetics, and density—seen by critics as overreach.
  • Voluntary private covenants can replace zoning: Advocates argue that neighborhood associations, real estate contracts, or homeowner agreements could handle many concerns without government mandates.
  • Reduces arbitrary government control: Zoning boards and planning commissions can be slow, politicized, and influenced by special interests. Eliminating zoning disperses decision-making to the individual level.

> Argument: Market-based signaling (e.g., homeowners choosing areas based on quality of life, or price adjustments for less-desirable locations) can internalize externalities better than top-down rules.

5. Reduced Inequality and Exclusion

Benefit:
Zoning—especially single-family zoning—is criticized for entrenching segregation by income, race, and opportunity.

  • Affordable housing becomes more geographically dispersed. Low- and middle-income households can move into high-opportunity neighborhoods without being restricted to "multi-family only" zones.
  • Opposition to exclusionary practices: Single-family zoning was historically used to enforce racial and class segregation (e.g., 20th-century U.S. "redlining" and racial covenants). Ending zoning allows integration through market forces and diverse housing types.

6. Efficiency and Market Responsiveness

Benefit:
Markets adapt faster than central planning.

  • Price signals guide development: If demand for apartments rises, landowners offer apartments. If people want live-work spaces, they can build them.
  • Reduced bureaucracy: Permitting and approvals under zoning systems are slow, costly, and favor large developers. Abolishing zoning could reduce delays and costs, enabling "permissionless" development in benign cases.

> Modern analog: "Home-rule" cities with light-touch regulations (e.g., Houston, Chattanooga) show that cities can function well without traditional Euclidean zoning.

Important Considerations & Counterpoints (Caveats)

While eliminating all zoning is radical, it’s important to note:

  • Nuisance regulation still valid: Advocates of deregulation don’t eliminate all land use rules. Nuisance law (e.g., preventing toxic dumping, excessive noise) remains to handle true harm.
  • Private alternatives exist: Voluntary covenants, community agreements, and insurance markets can handle many coordination issues.
  • Transitional risks: Sudden elimination could cause instability. Phased reforms (e.g., legalizing ADUs, upzoning, form-based codes) are often more politically and practically feasible.
  • Externalities: Some coordination (e.g., building safety, access to light/air, flood zones) may still benefit from minimal rules—but these could be achieved with simpler, targeted regulations.

Conclusion

Completely eliminating zoning laws could:

  • Unleash vast new housing supply, lowering prices and improving affordability.
  • Restore property rights by allowing owners to use their land as they see fit.
  • Create more dynamic, mixed, and inclusive cities where neighborhoods adapt naturally to needs.
  • Reduce government overreach and inefficient bureaucratic control.

While not without risks and downsides (e.g., potential for localized negative externalities, challenges in infrastructure planning), the argument for removing zoning laws is fundamentally an argument for human freedom, market responsiveness, and supply-driven solutions to the housing crisis. As urban economist Edberd Glaeser stated:
> "The most important housing regulation isn't the price of construction—it's whether the government will let you build at all."

In that light, eliminating zoning becomes not just an economic reform, but a pro-liberty, pro-equity, and pro-growth policy. Most reformers today advocate for relaxing not abolishing zoning entirely—but push toward a future where land use is guided more by markets than mandates.

You want to open a K-12 school in your home? Do it.

Abolish zoning.
Let the soil of our cities breathe again.
Let capital flow where it is needed.
Let innovation rise.
Let dirt become home.

Today.
Together.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for completely eliminating zoning laws, describing how removing all government land use regulations could improve housing availability, affordability, and respect for property rights.
Model Response:

Here are the main arguments made by proponents of completely eliminating zoning and government land-use regulations, and how they believe this would improve housing supply, affordability, and property rights.

  1. Large increase in housing supply
  • By-right building everywhere: Without zoning constraints on density, height, use, parking, lot size, setbacks, or floor-area ratios, property owners could add units, subdivide lots, and redevelop underused land far more easily. This removes “artificial scarcity” created by zoning.
  • Faster, cheaper permitting: Eliminating discretionary review, conditional use permits, variances, and environmental process layering would reduce time and risk, making more projects viable. Lower soft costs and shorter timelines increase output.
  • Land reallocation to highest-value uses: Markets would direct land toward the uses and intensities most demanded, enabling residential infill, mixed-use, and conversions of low-value commercial/industrial sites into housing where demand is strongest.
  • Incremental infill and “missing middle”: Small-scale builders and homeowners could add ADUs, duplexes, fourplexes, and rooming houses across existing neighborhoods—restoring organic growth patterns that historically produced abundant workforce housing.
  1. Lower housing costs and greater affordability
  • Supply-demand effect: More homes at all price tiers eases overall scarcity, moderating rents and sale prices. Elastic supply is the most robust long-run affordability tool.
  • Reduced development costs: Fewer regulatory hurdles mean less carrying cost, legal expense, compliance burden, and uncertainty premiums; those savings can pass through to prices.
  • Smaller, more varied units: Freedom to build smaller units, co-living, boarding houses, SROs, micro-units, and modular typologies expands options at lower price points, especially for singles, students, and lower-income households.
  • Mixed-use efficiencies: Allowing residential over shops or live-work reduces travel costs and supports car-free or car-light living, lowering total housing-plus-transportation costs.
  • Competition and innovation: Open entry for new builders and models (factory-built homes, shared housing platforms, land trusts) increases competitive pressure to deliver low-cost options.
  1. Greater respect for property rights and individual liberty
  • Owner autonomy: Property owners decide how to use and develop their land without needing permission for harmless activities. This aligns land use with voluntary exchange rather than political approval.
  • Protection from exclusionary practices: Zoning has historically been used to exclude lower-income residents and minorities via large lot sizes, bans on apartments, and parking mandates. Eliminating it curtails government-enabled exclusion.
  • Fewer arbitrary or politicized decisions: Removing discretionary review limits NIMBY veto power and reduces opportunities for favoritism or rent-seeking tied to entitlements and upzonings.
  1. Economic productivity and environmental benefits
  • Agglomeration and access: Allowing more homes near jobs improves labor-market matching and economic output. People can live closer to opportunity, boosting wages and reducing commuting time.
  • Lower emissions via density: More infill in high-demand, transit-served areas shortens trips, supports walking/cycling/transit, and reduces per-capita energy use and emissions.
  • Adaptive reuse and resilience: As demand shifts (e.g., retail to residential), rapid conversions reduce vacancies and blight, keeping urban fabric productive.
  1. Neighborhood diversity and social inclusion
  • Housing choice: A wider range of types and price points supports diverse households—seniors, multigenerational families, students, young workers—within the same neighborhoods.
  • Organic evolution: Instead of freezing neighborhoods in time, incremental changes allow places to adapt to demographic and economic realities.
  1. Administrative simplicity and reduced public cost
  • Streamlined governance: Eliminating complex zoning codes, variances, and enforcement reduces bureaucratic overhead and litigation.
  • Predictability through markets: Prices convey information and coordinate land use without elaborate regulatory apparatus.

Common responses to concerns (from proponents’ perspective)

  • Externalities and nuisances: Use general nuisance law, building and fire codes, and targeted rules for genuine health/safety impacts rather than broad use-separation. Private covenants and HOA rules can handle finer-grained preferences.
  • Infrastructure strain: Fund infrastructure with transparent user fees, special assessments, or connection charges rather than limiting housing through zoning. Pricing helps align capacity with demand.
  • Historic or environmental protection: Protect truly significant resources via narrow, well-defined designations and performance standards, not blanket prohibitions on housing.
  • Market cycles and displacement: Mitigate with portable subsidies (vouchers), cash assistance, and social housing production if desired—while keeping supply flexible to reduce pressure overall.

Bottom line Advocates argue that abolishing zoning would unleash large-scale, bottom-up housing production; lower costs through speed, competition, and variety; honor property rights; and allow cities to adapt dynamically. They see most current affordability and scarcity problems as products of regulatory constraints and believe that removing them would restore the traditional, incremental city-building that historically produced abundant, attainable housing.

Friends, neighbors, and fellow citizens,

We stand today at a crossroads between a past defined by arbitrary constraints and a future defined by opportunity, affordability, and freedom. For over a century, zoning laws have promised order and prosperity. Instead, they have delivered scarcity, segregation, higher costs, and a stifling of human potential. It’s time to be honest: zoning as we know it is a barrier to progress. If we want abundant housing, thriving neighborhoods, and true respect for individual liberty, we must abolish zoning laws entirely.

Zoning was built on a premise of control—of deciding from above what people may build, where they may live, and how communities must look. But the reality on the ground is undeniable: zoning inflates housing prices by restricting supply. It blocks new homes where people want to live, pushes growth outward, lengthens commutes, and chokes opportunity. It tells a property owner they may not add a duplex, a corner store, a mother-in-law unit, or a small apartment building—even when there is no harm to neighbors, and the demand is obvious. Zoning substitutes political gatekeeping for individual judgment and voluntary exchange.

Abolishing zoning is not an act of chaos. It is an act of trust—trust in people, in markets, and in the fundamental right to use one’s property without begging for permission. When we repeal zoning, we say yes to families who want to build an accessory unit to help pay the mortgage or house a relative. We say yes to small developers who can add missing-middle housing that blends seamlessly into neighborhoods. We say yes to corner cafes and walkable streets that emerge organically, not by decree. We say yes to more homes—of all types, at all price points—so that teachers, nurses, service workers, and young families can live near the jobs and schools they depend on.

The free market, guided by millions of individual decisions, is the most powerful engine for aligning what is built with what people actually want. Zoning throttles that engine. Consider the consequences we see all around us: sky-high rents, half-empty office corridors that cannot be easily repurposed, and neighborhoods frozen in amber while the next generation is priced out. We cannot plan our way out of a housing shortage created by planning. We must unleash creation.

Some will warn that abolishing zoning will erode neighborhood character or overwhelm infrastructure. But character is not a museum exhibit; it is a living tapestry woven by the people who inhabit it. And infrastructure can and should be governed by straightforward, content-neutral standards—like building codes for safety, noise and nuisance rules, and simple, transparent impact fees tied to actual costs. We don’t need zoning to keep homes safe or streets functional. We need clear rules focused on real harms, not blanket prohibitions that freeze communities in time.

Others will say: What about equity? Zoning has been one of the most powerful tools of exclusion in our history. It has walled off opportunity, hardened segregation, and protected privilege by restricting what can be built—and for whom. Abolishing zoning is a moral imperative. It opens the door to more homes in high-opportunity areas, reduces displacement pressure by allowing supply to meet demand, and restores the right of every person to live closer to jobs, schools, and transit. Abundance is equity. Choice is dignity. Freedom is fairness.

Imagine a city where vacant lots become homes, where office buildings convert to apartments without years of hearings, where homeowners can add gentle density, and where the cost of shelter falls because we finally allowed builders to build. Imagine entrepreneurs revitalizing corridors with mixed-use buildings, childcare centers, and small businesses—because they are free to meet community needs without navigating a gauntlet of prohibitions. Imagine an end to endless battles over permits, variances, and spot rezonings that reward insiders and lobbyists while shutting out everyone else.

This is not a leap into the unknown. It is a return to first principles. Protect people from harm, not from change. Protect safety through codes, not exclusion through zoning. Protect neighbors from nuisances, not from new neighbors. Replace discretionary veto points with predictable, objective rules. Replace ceilings with horizons.

We can do this. We can choose freedom over fear, abundance over artificial scarcity, and human flourishing over bureaucratic stagnation. We can abolish zoning and, in doing so, give our children a fairer shot at a home, a business, a future.

Let’s open the gates. Let’s build. Let’s trust people and the power of voluntary cooperation. Abolish zoning—fully, finally, and for the benefit of all.

Title: Unshackling the Skyline: The Moral and Economic Imperative to Abolish Zoning

Introduction

Since the early 20th century, the map of the modern city has been drawn not by the organic flow of human interaction or the logic of the market, but by the red pen of the municipal bureaucrat. Zoning laws—those invisible cages of regulation that dictate where one may live, work, and trade—have become the silent architects of our societal ills. While ostensibly designed to protect health and safety, these regulations have calcified into a system that stifles economic dynamism, entrenches inequality, and renders housing unaffordable for millions. To solve the housing crisis, revive local economies, and restore the fundamental right to property, we must take the radical but necessary step of abolishing all zoning laws entirely. Only by unleashing unrestricted, market-driven development can we build a society that is both prosperous and free.

The Economic Stagnation of the "Monoculture"

The primary argument for abolishing zoning is the restoration of economic efficiency. Modern zoning—particularly Euclidean zoning, which separates land use into exclusive categories like residential, commercial, and industrial—assumes a static world. It creates urban "monocultures" where a neighborhood is strictly sleeping quarters and another is strictly office space. This artificial separation forces citizens to commute vast distances, clogging infrastructure and wasting hours of productive time.

Without zoning, the free market would naturally evolve into a mixed-use utopia. The corner store would once again sit beneath the apartment; the bakery would neighbor the workshop. This density is the lifeblood of vibrant economies. When the government dictates that land must remain a single-family estate, it artificially constrains supply and kills the "agglomeration effects" that drive innovation. By allowing unrestricted development, we permit the natural concentration of talent and commerce, fostering a dynamic environment where businesses can start and grow without the prohibitive costs of navigating zoning boards.

Housing Affordability and the Right to Build

Perhaps the most urgent moral argument for abolition is the housing affordability crisis. Zoning is the root cause of this scarcity. By restricting the height, density, and type of buildings that can be constructed, governments have artificially strangled the supply of housing. In many major cities, it is illegal to build anything other than a single-family home on the vast majority of land.

When the supply of housing is capped by law, but the demand to live in productive cities continues to rise, prices inevitably skyrocket. This is not a market failure; it is a regulatory failure. Abolishing zoning would allow the market to respond to high demand with high supply. We would see the rapid construction of high-density apartments and affordable starter homes to meet the needs of the population. When developers are free to build up and build dense, the cost of shelter drops, moving housing from a luxury asset back to a basic commodity. To deny people the ability to build homes on their own land is a violation of their liberty and a cruelty to those who cannot afford the artificially inflated prices of the status quo.

Restoring Property Rights

At its core, the argument against zoning is a defense of property rights. Property rights are fundamental to a free society, yet zoning laws represent the state’s usurpation of these rights. When a government tells a property owner they cannot convert their garage into an office, or build a duplex on a vacant lot, they are effectively expropriating that land for a public purpose—social engineering—without compensation.

Abolishing zoning restores the sanctity of the deed. It affirms that the individual owner, not the collective, has the ultimate say in how their property is used. This shift promotes a high-trust society, assuming that individuals are capable of negotiating with their neighbors through nuisance laws and contracts, rather than requiring pre-emptive prohibition.

Addressing the Counter-Argument: Externalities and Nuisance

Critics will inevitably argue that without zoning, a slaughterhouse could open next to a nursery, destroying quality of life. This argument relies on a misunderstanding of market forces and common law. In a free market, the value of property is derived from its desirability. No rational investor would open a noisy, noxious factory in a high-value residential district, as they would immediately face opposition from other high-value stakeholders. Furthermore, the legal framework of "nuisance" already exists to protect citizens from actual harm (pollution, noise, danger) without the need for the broad, prophylactic brush of zoning.

We do not need zoning to prevent factories from poisoning neighborhoods; we need robust enforcement of property rights and environmental safety. Zoning is a clumsy tool that solves a problem that market dynamics and tort law can handle far more elegantly.

Conclusion

Zoning laws are relics of a top-down philosophy that views citizens as subjects to be managed rather than agents to be freed. They have created artificial scarcity, destroyed neighborhood character through rigid separation, and priced the working class out of their own cities. The path forward requires courage. We must trust in the emergent order of the market rather than the imposed order of the planner. By abolishing zoning, we do not invite chaos; we invite vitality, affordability, and liberty. We allow the city to breathe again, unlocking the potential for a dense, interconnected, and flourishing human civilization. It is time to tear down the fences.

Of course. Let's explore the theoretical and practical arguments for a radical approach to land use: the complete elimination of zoning laws. This idea, often associated with the "strong town" movement and advocates for housing deregulation, posits that removing all government-imposed land use regulations would lead to a more efficient, affordable, and property-rights-respecting urban environment.

Here is a breakdown of the proposed benefits and the reasoning behind them.

1. Dramatically Increased Housing Supply and Affordability

The Reasoning: Zoning laws are seen as a primary constraint on the housing market. By legally prohibiting the construction of anything other than single-family detached homes in vast swaths of cities, zoning artificially limits the number of homes that can be built. This is described as a "supply stranglehold."

  • Mechanism: Removing these laws would allow the market to respond to demand. If an area has high housing demand (and thus high prices), developers could respond by building more units on a single lot—such as duplexes, fourplexes, apartment buildings, or mixed-use structures. This natural, demand-driven increase in density is called "gentle density" or "infill development."
  • The Beneficiary: This increased supply is theorized to directly combat the housing crisis by making more homes available, which should, in a free market, put downward pressure on both rents and purchase prices. It would also diversify the housing stock, offering more options like townhomes, courtyard apartments, and smaller units that cater to different income levels and family sizes.

The Counter-Consideration: Skeptics argue that this assumes landowners will choose to build more affordable, dense housing. In high-value neighborhoods, the land itself is so expensive that the most profitable development might still be luxury housing. Additionally, without infrastructure requirements tied to development (a function of zoning and related codes), new density could overwhelm schools, sewage systems, and transportation networks.

2. Unfettered Respect for Property Rights

The Reasoning: This is the core philosophical argument. Proponents contend that zoning is an improper government infringement on the fundamental right of a property owner to use their land as they see fit.

  • Mechanism: The argument is straightforward: if you own a piece of land, you should have the right to build what you want on it, as long as you do not directly harm your neighbors (e.g., through pollution, excessive noise, or by physically encroaching on their property). Zoning, by telling a homeowner they cannot build a duplex or an apartment, is seen as an unjust "taking" of economic potential without compensation.
  • The Beneficiary: This maximizes individual liberty and economic freedom. Property owners can respond to their own needs and market signals without seeking government permission for a list of approved uses.

The Counter-Consideration: The concept of "harm" is contested. A major criticism is the "nuisance" problem. Does building a high-rise apartment next to a single-family home cause "harm" by changing the character of the neighborhood, increasing traffic, blocking sunlight, or lowering the perceived property value of neighbors? Current zoning exists precisely to prevent these kinds of large-scale changes that a majority of existing residents find undesirable. The property rights of the one owner conflict with the collective "property rights" and lifestyle expectations of the many existing neighbors.

3. More Vibrant, Walkable, and Economically Dynamic Communities

The Reasoning: Zoning, particularly post-WWII, has led to the strict separation of land uses—residential here, commercial there, industrial over there. This is blamed for creating sterile, car-dependent suburbs.

  • Mechanism: Eliminating zoning would allow for mixed-use development. A ground-floor retail shop could sit below apartments. A home-based business (like a bakery or workshop) could legally operate from a residence. This organic mix is how most historic, beloved urban neighborhoods developed. It creates "eyes on the street" for safety, supports local small businesses, and allows people to live closer to where they work and shop, potentially reducing car dependency.
  • The Beneficiary: The community as a whole benefits from increased convenience, local economic activity, and a more interesting, human-scaled environment. It could also be more environmentally sustainable by reducing long commutes.

The Counter-Consideration: Opponents argue this leads to conflict and a decline in quality of life. Imagine a noisy bar opening in a residential building, or a factory emitting fumes next to a playground. They argue that some separation of heavy industry and dense commercial activity from residential areas is necessary for health, safety, and peaceful enjoyment of one's home. The predictability of zoning is seen as a feature, not a bug, for community planning.

4. Reduction in Corruption and Government Overreach

The Reasoning: The process of getting zoning variances or rezoning a parcel is often slow, expensive, and opaque. It involves petitions, public hearings, and votes by planning commissions and city councils.

  • Mechanism: This process creates a "permission structure" that is ripe for corruption and cronyism. Developers with political connections or deep pockets can navigate the system more easily. Large, politically connected landowners can use zoning to block competitors. Eliminating this discretionary process would create a more level playing field, governed by clear, objective rules (like building codes for safety) rather than subjective political approval.
  • The Beneficiary: Smaller developers and homeowners benefit from a simpler, more predictable system. The theoretical result is a fairer market where projects succeed or fail based on market demand and financial viability, not political connections.

The Counter-Consideration: The public hearing and review process, while flawed, is a democratic forum for community input. Complete elimination could lead to unchecked development that the public has no say in until it appears. It shifts power entirely to developers and landowners, who may have financial incentives that conflict with broader public interests like green space, affordable housing quotas, or historical preservation.

Conclusion: The Trade-Off

The debate over eliminating zoning is fundamentally a conflict between two visions of a city:

  1. The Free-Market Vision: A city as an organic, emergent system. Property rights are paramount, and the best use of land is determined by the invisible hand of the market. The result is theorized to be more affordable, dynamic, and responsive to human needs.
  2. The Community-Planned Vision: A city as a designed product. Collective decision-making through government regulations is necessary to shape a desirable environment, prevent nuisances, protect community character, and ensure orderly development for the common good.

Those advocating for eliminating zoning see current laws as a corrupt, exclusionary tool that stifles growth and tramples property rights, causing a housing crisis. Their opponents see zoning as a necessary, if imperfect, tool to protect quality of life, community values, and property values from the potentially chaotic and destructive forces of unchecked private development.

Model Response:

The Case for Abolishing Zoning

Introduction: An Experiment That Failed

For roughly a century, American cities have run an extraordinary experiment. In 1916, Berkeley, California adopted the nation's first single-family-only district. In 1926, the Supreme Court blessed comprehensive zoning in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a decision in which the district court had described apartment buildings as "mere parasites." Within two decades, nearly every significant American municipality had adopted a zoning code. Today, in most American cities, roughly three-quarters of residential land is legally off-limits to anything but detached single-family houses.

The experiment has run long enough to be evaluated. The verdict is devastating. Zoning has made housing unaffordable, entrenched racial and class segregation, throttled national economic growth, worsened environmental outcomes, and transferred trillions of dollars of wealth from the young and poor to the old and propertied. It has done so while failing to deliver the benefits its proponents promised, benefits that were, in most cases, already secured by other legal institutions.

The correct response is not another round of technocratic tinkering — another upzoning, another "missing middle" pilot, another state preemption bill with fourteen exemptions. The correct response is abolition. Zoning should be eliminated root and branch, and the regulation of land returned to the institutions that governed it before 1916 and that govern it still in the one large American city that never adopted it: nuisance law, private contract, and the ordinary common law of property.

I. Zoning's Original Sin Was Not Incidental

It is impossible to understand zoning without understanding what it was for. In 1917, the Supreme Court struck down explicitly racial zoning in Buchanan v. Warley. Municipalities did not abandon the goal; they changed the instrument. Planners and reformers of the era openly discussed density restrictions, minimum lot sizes, and apartment bans as means of achieving through economics what could no longer be achieved through explicit racial classification. The founding conference of the National Conference on City Planning and the trade literature of the 1920s are not subtle documents.

This history matters not because it makes zoning permanently guilty by association, but because the mechanism has never changed. A one-acre minimum lot size does not name a race. It simply prices out anyone who cannot afford an acre. A ban on multifamily housing does not name a class. It simply makes it illegal to build the housing types that non-wealthy people can afford. The tool works exactly as designed, which is why the geography of American segregation maps so precisely onto the geography of restrictive zoning, and why the most stringently zoned metropolitan areas — Boston, New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles — remain among the most racially and economically segregated in the country despite generations of liberal politics.

Defenders of zoning reform often say the system has been "misused." It has not been misused. It has been used.

II. The Economic Indictment

Consider the most basic fact in American housing economics: in heavily zoned metropolitan areas, the price of a house vastly exceeds the cost of building one. Economists Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko have documented this gap — sometimes called the "zoning tax" — and found it exceeds several hundred thousand dollars per unit in the most restricted markets. In an unconstrained market, that gap would be arbitraged away by construction. It persists only because construction is illegal.

The macroeconomic consequences are staggering. Chang-Tai Hsieh and Enrico Moretti, in research published in the American Economic Journal, estimated that if just three highly productive metros — New York, San Francisco, and San Jose — had relaxed their land use constraints to the level of the median American city, U.S. GDP would have been meaningfully higher, with aggregate worker wages rising by thousands of dollars annually. Their earlier estimates were larger still. The mechanism is simple and hard to dispute: America's most productive places have made it illegal for workers to move there. A machinist who could double her output by relocating from a struggling region to a booming one cannot, because the rent consumes the gain. Zoning has turned the American labor market from a fluid national system into a set of walled gardens.

The distributional consequences are worse than the aggregate ones. Zoning's costs fall on renters, young families, immigrants, and the poor. Its benefits accrue to existing homeowners, whose asset values are inflated by the artificial scarcity they vote to maintain. William Fischel's "homevoter hypothesis" describes this honestly: local land use politics is dominated by people whose largest financial asset appreciates when supply is suppressed. We have built a system of governance in which the incumbent beneficiaries of scarcity control the supply valve. No one designing institutions from scratch would do this.

And the human costs are not merely financial. Gregg Colburn and Clayton Page Aldern's research on homelessness found that regional homelessness rates are predicted far better by rents and vacancy rates than by poverty, mental illness, drug use, or climate. Cities with high rates of addiction and poverty but abundant housing have low homelessness. Cities with modest social problems and constricted housing markets have crises. Homelessness in America is, to a first approximation, a housing supply problem — which is to say, a zoning problem.

III. Zoning Fails on Its Own Terms

The standard justification for zoning is the separation of incompatible uses: no tannery beside the kindergarten. But observe how little of the modern zoning code has anything to do with this.

Height limits do not protect anyone from a tannery. Nor do floor-area ratios, setback requirements, minimum lot sizes, minimum parking requirements, unit-count caps, aesthetic review boards, or bans on duplexes in single-family districts. These provisions do not separate industry from housing; they separate housing from housing. They make it illegal to put two families where one family used to live. The genuinely noxious-use problem — the actual tannery — occupies perhaps five percent of the modern code and is in any case addressed far more effectively by environmental regulation, which targets emissions directly rather than by geographic proxy.

Meanwhile, zoning has produced enormous externalities of its own. By mandating low densities and separating homes from shops and jobs, it has made automobile dependence compulsory. Donald Shoup's work on parking minimums showed that requirements set by rule of thumb, with no empirical basis, have forced developers to build vast quantities of unwanted asphalt, raising housing costs and inducing driving. The resulting sprawl consumes farmland and habitat, and generates far higher per-capita carbon emissions than the compact urban development zoning forbids. Glaeser and Matthew Kahn found that America's greenest places by household carbon footprint are dense coastal cities — precisely the places where building is hardest. American zoning has systematically pushed population growth from low-emissions places to high-emissions places. It is, in aggregate, one of the most environmentally destructive policy regimes in the country, enacted largely by people who consider themselves environmentalists.

IV. What Replaces It: The Law Was Already There

The strongest objection to abolition is not that zoning is good but that its absence would be chaos. This objection rests on a misunderstanding of what zoning replaced.

Before 1916, land was governed. It was governed by the common law of nuisance, which for centuries had provided remedies against smoke, stench, noise, vibration, and interference with the use and enjoyment of neighboring property. It was governed by restrictive covenants and easements, through which owners could contractually bind themselves and successors to whatever land use terms they valued. It was governed by tort law, which imposed liability for the harms one's activities caused. And it continues to be governed by building codes, fire codes, and structural safety standards — which are entirely distinct from zoning and which no abolitionist proposes to repeal.

Zoning did not create order out of anarchy. It replaced a decentralized, adjudicative, harm-focused system with a centralized, prospective, categorical one. The difference is crucial. Nuisance law asks: is this activity actually harming you? Zoning asks: is this activity on the list? The first is calibrated to real injury. The second bans the construction of an apartment building on the theory that apartments are, in the abstract, a category of thing that some people dislike.

Private ordering is also far more flexible than its critics assume. Homeowners who genuinely value uniformity can purchase it: covenants, HOAs, and condominium regimes are contractual devices for exactly this purpose. The key distinction is between people buying restrictions on their own land and people voting restrictions onto their neighbors' land. The first is a property right. The second is a taking without compensation, dressed in the language of community.

V. The Empirical Record

We are not speculating. Houston, the fourth-largest city in the United States, has never adopted zoning. Its voters rejected it in 1948, 1962, and 1993. Bernard Siegan's classic study Land Use Without Zoning examined Houston in detail and found no descent into disorder: uses sorted themselves substantially by market forces, because land values, financing requirements, and reputational incentives all push toward compatible clustering without any need for a code to command it. Nobody builds a smelter next to a luxury condo tower, because the land is too expensive and the smelter operator would rather be somewhere cheap.

What Houston does have is housing. When the city reduced its minimum lot size from 5,000 square feet to 1,400 square feet inside the loop in 1998 — and citywide in 2013 — it triggered the construction of tens of thousands of townhomes, delivering ownership opportunities at price points that have simply ceased to exist in coastal metros. Houston metro has at times permitted more housing units in a year than the entire state of California, with three times Houston's population. Its median home price sits at a fraction of San Francisco's or Boston's, in a city with a booming economy and a growing population. Houston is not a paradise, and its remaining regulations (parking minimums, setbacks, deed restrictions) impose real costs. But it is decisive evidence that a large, complex, wealthy American city can function without zoning, and that the primary difference it makes is affordability.

Internationally, the gradient runs the same direction. Tokyo, where land use is regulated at the national level with permissive, form-based standards and minimal local veto power, permits well over 100,000 housing units annually — more than the entire state of California — and has seen real rents remain roughly flat for decades in one of the world's most desirable cities. The correlation between regulatory restrictiveness and housing costs is one of the most robust findings in urban economics.

VI. Why Reform Is Not Enough

One might concede all of this and still argue for reform rather than abolition. This is a mistake, for a structural reason: discretionary permitting systems are inherently capturable.

Every zoning code that survives becomes a menu of veto points. Every carve-out becomes a hook. Every "public input" requirement becomes a delay mechanism, and delay is denial in a business financed by construction loans. California has passed dozens of housing reform bills over fifteen years; the marginal project still faces environmental review litigation, design review, historic determinations, and appeals. The reason is not that legislators drafted badly. It is that any system requiring case-by-case permission concentrates the costs of a project on identifiable neighbors while diffusing its benefits across strangers who do not yet live there and cannot vote. That asymmetry will defeat any procedural fix you devise. The only durable solution is to remove the permission requirement itself.

Abolition also has a virtue that reform lacks: it is simple, legible, and hard to game. "You may build on your land, subject to building codes, environmental law, and liability for nuisance" is a rule a small developer can understand without hiring a land use attorney. The current system's complexity is itself a barrier to entry that favors large, politically connected firms over the small builders who once produced most American housing.

VII. The Moral Argument

Strip away the economics and a simpler claim remains. If you own a plot of land, the presumption should be that you may build on it. Not that you may build after persuading a commission, appeasing a neighborhood association, funding a traffic study, and surviving a hearing at which people who own nothing on your parcel explain that your project is out of character.

The current arrangement inverts the basic logic of property. Your neighbors have effectively acquired an option over the use of your land — a valuable property interest — for free. And the people most harmed by this arrangement are precisely those with no standing to object: the family that would have moved to the city if housing existed, the young worker priced into a two-hour commute, the immigrant, the person whose life would have gone differently in a country where the productive places were open. They do not attend hearings, because they are not there. Zoning's defining feature is that its victims are invisible at the moment of decision.

A regime of full property rights does not mean a regime of no rules. It means rules that respond to demonstrated harm rather than speculative aesthetic preference, that bind through contract rather than through the coerced consent of the absent, and that treat the right to build as a right rather than a privilege dispensed by committee.

Conclusion

Zoning was born of prejudice, sustained by rent-seeking, and defended by arguments that do not survive contact with either economic evidence or legal history. It has raised the cost of shelter, the most basic human need, above the reach of tens of millions of people. It has stranded workers away from opportunity, driven a national homelessness crisis, and accelerated environmental damage in the name of protecting the environment. And it has done all this while providing benefits that nuisance law, building codes, environmental regulation, and private covenants already provide better.

A century is long enough. Repeal the codes. Return land use to property owners, contract, and the law of harm. Let cities do what they did for millennia before planners discovered the map and the colored pencil: grow.

Note: This is a one-sided advocacy piece written to your specification. The strongest counterarguments — concerning genuine externalities that nuisance litigation handles poorly, infrastructure and utility coordination, the transition costs of abandoning reliance interests, and the historical role of private covenants in enforcing racial exclusion — deserve serious engagement, and I'm happy to write the opposing case or a balanced analysis if that would be useful.
